title: The maid who welcomed the sage
hookLine: the younger widow turns pale, the elder sends her maid instead, and the maid's welcome gives the palace its wisest son
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god
tomorrow: a princess learns her groom is blind, and takes a vow.

cards: Same palace, same sage, a different widow. Satyavati sends Vyasa to the younger princess, Ambalika. When she sees him, the blood leaves her face.
She doesn't shut her eyes, as her sister did; her fear shows on her face instead. And the Kuru house is about to get three brothers: the blind one, the pale one, and one nobody planned for at all.

teach.b: Vyasa tells his mother: because she turned pale, the son will be pale. Pandu, the pale one. Satyavati asks for one more son from the elder widow.
But Ambika can't face him again. She dresses her maid in her own jewels and sends her instead. The maid isn't afraid.

teach.h: THE MAID RISES AND GREETS HIM.
teach.b: She rises when the sage comes in, greets him with respect, and serves him. Vyasa is pleased. You are no longer a servant, he tells her, and your son will be virtuous and wise.

teach.h: VIDURA, DHARMA BORN AS A MAN.
teach.b: That son is Vidura, and the text later says he is Dharma itself, the god of what's right, born as a man. So, three brothers: one who can't see, one who's pale, and the wisest, born to the woman everyone else overlooked.

Hindus have a name for what she did. Atithi devo bhava: let the guest be God to you. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad, part of a teacher's parting advice to students, beside honoring mother, father and teacher.
The princesses saw a frightening stranger. The maid saw someone to honor, and her life changed.
Many teachers read it this way: the welcome itself is worship.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.
teach.b: That's why, in many Hindu homes, a guest gets water before asking, the best seat, and the first plate, even unannounced, even when there's little to give.
Today it's the friend who drops by and leaves full, or the new kid you wave over to your table. In this tradition, how you greet the one at your door is part of how you greet God.

how: Atithi devo bhava, from the Taittiriya Upanishad, is still taught to Hindu children and lived at the door: water first, the best seat, a full plate. Vidura's later counsel, the Vidura Niti, is read by some Hindus as a guide to wise living.

o: the sage's son who went back to the forest
the strong one, named for his mighty arms
the pale one, born to the frightened Ambalika

games.q: three brothers and a welcome — tap the pairs.
p: the maid's son, Dharma born as a man
rose and greeted the sage with respect
let the guest be God to you

s: Ambika went to Vyasa a second time
she sent her maid, dressed in her own ornaments.
atithi devo bhava means guests should honor the host
it runs the other way: the host welcomes the guest as God.
the text says Vidura is Dharma born as a man
under a sage's curse, a story for another day.

games.q: Sam drops by right at dinner. it's leftovers and the house is a mess. by the maid's story, what fits?
o: water first, a seat, and a plate, mess and all.
say it's a bad time; guests deserve a clean house.
let him in, but don't offer food; it's only leftovers.
games.why: atithi devo bhava. the maid had no palace of her own, only respect, and she gave it. the welcome is the worship, not the house.

practice: Bring to mind who might come to your door this week: a friend, a neighbor, a relative you find hard. Picture greeting them the way the maid did: standing up, a glass of water, a real hello.
If you pray, offer a little water or food at your altar or in your heart first, as many Hindus do before eating. If you don't, just choose one small welcome you'll give.

wordCard.voice: Pandu, the pale one, born because his mother's face went white; brother to the blind Dhritarashtra and the wise Vidura.

orig.note: Sanskrit Pandu: the pale one, the name Vyasa gives Ambalika's son because she turned pale.

carryVoice: Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. A maid's welcome gave the palace its wisest son. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Ambalika and the birth of Pandu; the maid sent by Ambika and the birth of Vidura)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Vidura as Dharma, cursed by the sage Animandavya)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (the teacher's parting instruction: mother, father, teacher and guest each as God; atithi devo bhava)
